title: Exhuming McCarthy
description: A jaunty, horn-punched protest song with a dark joke at its core: R.E.M. dig up 1950s red-baiter Senator Joseph McCarthy and hold him up as a mirror to Reagan-era America.

pops.text: That clatter at the start is a manual typewriter — reportedly the very one Michael Stipe used to write the band's lyrics at the time.
The title digs up Senator Joseph McCarthy, whose 1950s anti-communist witch hunts gave the English language the word 'McCarthyism.'
Stipe draws the line straight from the 1950s to 1987, name-checking the spirit of the Iran-Contra era: 'Look who bought the myth — by jingo, buy American.'
Mid-song you hear a real piece of history: Army counsel Joseph Welch rebuking McCarthy at the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings — 'Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last?'
Welch's line landed on June 9, 1954, defending a young lawyer on his staff, and it is still one of the most quoted put-downs in American politics.
Guitarist Peter Buck said in 1987 that it felt like the kind of year Joe McCarthy would come back — and be hailed as a hero.
Mike Mills sings the hook line 'It's a sign of the times' — a nod in the direction of Prince's Sign o' the Times, released while Document was being made.
The song sits on Document, R.E.M.'s fifth album — billed on the sleeve as 'R.E.M. No. 5' — released in the late summer of 1987.
Document was the band's first album with producer Scott Litt, the start of a partnership that ran through six records, including Out of Time and Automatic for the People.
By January 1988 Document had gone platinum — R.E.M.'s first million-selling album, and the record that carried them from college radio toward the mainstream.

title: You Are the Everything
description: A hushed, cricket-filled night song from Green: Peter Buck picks up a mandolin, the band swaps instruments, and Michael Stipe delivers one of his first straight, unironic love songs.

pops.text: Listen at the very start: the song opens with the sound of crickets on a warm Southern night before any instrument comes in.
This is a game of musical chairs — Peter Buck plays mandolin, drummer Bill Berry plays bass, and bassist Mike Mills moves to accordion.
Buck's mandolin was an oddly shaped Italian mandolin-cum-lyre he had bought in 1987; Green was the first R.E.M. album to feature it.
Stipe asked his bandmates not to write any 'R.E.M.-type songs' for this album — Berry later joked the new method was to grab an instrument you can't play and fool around until it sounds right.
Critics often call this Stipe's first blatant love song without irony: 'Sometimes I feel like I can't even sing — I'm very scared for this world, I'm very scared for me.'
The mandolin experiment started here and on two sister tracks, 'The Wrong Child' and 'Hairshirt' — the template for 'Losing My Religion' three years later.
It is track 3 on Green, R.E.M.'s sixth album and their major-label debut for Warner Bros., released in November 1988.
Green was recorded in 1988 at Ardent Studios in Memphis and Bearsville Studios in Woodstock, New York, again with producer Scott Litt.
The official video is drawn from Tourfilm, the concert film of the band's 1989 Green world tour — the tour that turned R.E.M. into an arena act.
The song's quiet pastoral mood points ahead: reviewers hear it as the bridge to the autumnal hush of Out of Time and Automatic for the People.

title: Emotional Rescue
description: Mick Jagger goes full falsetto over a slinky disco-funk groove, and the Stones score one of their most unlikely hits — complete with a heat-vision promo video as strange as the song.

pops.text: That high, floating vocal is Mick Jagger in falsetto — he wrote the song on electric piano and sang it that way from the very first demo.
The falsetto nods to the disco era: the Bee Gees' hits and Marvin Gaye's 'Got to Give It Up' are the comparisons critics reached for in 1980.
Surprise in the credits: Ronnie Wood plays bass on this track, while regular bassist Bill Wyman plays synthesizer.
The smooth saxophone lines come from Bobby Keys, the Stones' longtime horn man, who reportedly did a double-take at Jagger's 'Minnie Mouse' vocal.
It was recorded in October 1979, across sessions split between Compass Point in the Bahamas and Pathé Marconi in Paris.
Released as the lead single on 20 June 1980, it reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 9 in the UK.
The album of the same name topped the Billboard chart for seven weeks that summer — the Stones' first UK No. 1 album since Goats Head Soup.
The official promo uses thermal-imaging 'heat vision' effects, matching the heat-map faces on the album's poster and sleeve artwork.
Hardcore fans grumbled about the Stones going disco — a debate they had already started two years earlier with 'Miss You.'
Amazingly, the band did not play the song live for 33 years: its concert debut finally came on 3 May 2013 in Los Angeles.

title: Postcard
description: A bright, anthemic road song from the Athens, Georgia jam band's third album — a letter home sung over rolling guitars, written years before it ever reached a studio.

pops.text: 'Well, I've been sittin' here, thinkin' about you' — the whole song is framed as a postcard home from the road, sung by frontman John Bell.
Postcard is one of the band's oldest originals: it was already in Widespread Panic's live sets back in 1986, in their Uptown Lounge days in Athens.
The writing credit is shared between the band and Thomas Guenther — one of the few outside names in the Everyday songwriting credits.
It finally got a studio recording as track 10 on Everyday, the band's third album, released by Capricorn Records in March 1993.
Everyday was recorded at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Sheffield, Alabama, with producer Johnny Sandlin.
The album was the first to feature keyboardist John 'JoJo' Hermann as a full member — the record that locked in the band's classic lineup.
Album sessions ran through Christmas 1992; drummer Todd Nance joked that giving up Christmas to finish might make 'every day' Christmas — and the album got its title.
Look at the Everyday cover sometime: the model pictured is a then-unknown Angelina Jolie.
Everyday reached No. 184 on the Billboard 200 and the Top 10 of the Heatseekers chart — modest numbers for a band built on relentless touring.

The band's Athens roots run deep: fellow Athenian Vic Chesnutt later recorded two albums with Panic members as brute., and the band still returns to 'Postcard' on stage decades later, including their 25th-anniversary Athens shows in 2011.

title: Beauty and the Beast
description: Mrs. Potts the teapot sings Belle and the Beast into their first dance — Angela Lansbury's warm, grandmotherly title ballad for Disney's 1991 masterpiece, recorded in a single legendary take.

pops.text: The singer is Angela Lansbury as Mrs. Potts, the enchanted teapot — a role she took twenty years after starring in Disney's Bedknobs and Broomsticks.
Lansbury doubted the song suited her ageing voice and only agreed to record one take as a guide — that single take is the one in the film.
Her flight to the session had been diverted by a bomb scare, and she arrived after an all-night journey — then nailed it in one try, moving the studio to tears.
The song was written by lyricist Howard Ashman and composer Alan Menken, the team behind The Little Mermaid.
Menken said he devoted more time to this title song than to any other number in the film.
In the film it plays over the famous ballroom dance — a sweeping sequence built around a computer-generated ballroom and a camera that swoops in 3D, a landmark for Disney animation.
The film itself was historic: the first animated feature ever nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture.
The song won the Academy Award and the Golden Globe for Best Original Song, plus Grammy Awards including Best Song Written for Visual Media.
Howard Ashman died in March 1991, eight months before the film opened; the movie is dedicated to him, and his partner accepted his Oscar.
A pop duet version by Celine Dion and Peabo Bryson played over the end credits and became a hit single in its own right.

title: Remember Me
description: Ernesto de la Cruz, the Land of the Dead's biggest star, belts his signature song in full mariachi splendour — Benjamin Bratt's show-stopping version from Pixar's Coco.

pops.text: This is the Ernesto de la Cruz version: a grand, old-Hollywood-style spectacle number, performed by Benjamin Bratt as the film's musical idol.
Bratt had no professional singing background; he prepared by studying the charro films and ranchera stars of Mexico's Golden Age of cinema.
'Remember Me' was written by Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez — the married team who won an Oscar for Frozen's 'Let It Go.'
The writers designed the lyric to work several ways: as Ernesto's showpiece, as Héctor's tender lullaby to his daughter, and as Miguel's reunion song.
Anderson-Lopez said the song is written from the viewpoint of someone hoping to be remembered by a loved one — its meaning changes with tempo and tone.
In the story, Ernesto made the song world-famous — but the film slowly reveals Héctor, his old partner, was its true composer.
The soundtrack album opens with this track; the same song returns as 'Remember Me (Lullaby)' and 'Remember Me (Reunion)' later in the film.
Over the end credits, Miguel and Natalia Lafourcade sing a pop duet version, in English and Spanish.
'Remember Me' won the Academy Award for Best Original Song, giving the Lopezes their second Oscar.
Coco also won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and its score — weaving the song's melody throughout — is by Michael Giacchino.

title: China Girl
description: Bowie reclaims his own co-write from Iggy Pop, Nile Rodgers gives it a gleaming pop shine, Stevie Ray Vaughan lets rip — and the Sydney-shot video becomes an MTV-era landmark.

pops.text: Bowie didn't write this one alone, or first: he and Iggy Pop wrote it in 1976, and Pop released it on his debut solo album The Idiot in 1977.
The pair drafted it — working title 'Borderline' — at the Château d'Hérouville in France, where Bowie was producing Pop's album.
Pop's lyric was inspired by Kuelan Nguyen, a Vietnamese woman at the studio; his version was dark and brooding, and it never charted.
Bowie revived the song for Let's Dance partly to help Pop, who was struggling financially — a hit remake meant real royalty money.
Producer Nile Rodgers rebuilt it around a bright, Asian-tinged guitar riff; he later said he feared the riff was too jokey — Bowie loved it and called it fantastic.
The lead guitar is a young Stevie Ray Vaughan, whose own debut album Texas Flood arrived the same season as Let's Dance.
Released as the album's second single on 31 May 1983, it reached No. 2 in the UK — held off the top by The Police's 'Every Breath You Take' — and No. 10 in the US.
The video, directed by David Mallet, was shot mainly in Sydney's Chinatown and starred New Zealand model Geeling Ng.
Bowie described the video as a very simple, very direct statement against racism; its beach finale quotes the famous surf scene from From Here to Eternity.
Let's Dance became one of Bowie's biggest albums ever — his first US platinum record — and 'China Girl' remains its second-most-remembered single.

title: Daylight
description: The opening track of Rosemary, the Chapel Hill band's debut album: cascading guitars, Greg Humphreys' soulful vocal, and a chorus begging the dawn to break — pure North Carolina jangle-pop.

pops.text: 'Daylight' opens Rosemary, the 1992 debut album by Chapel Hill, North Carolina band Dillon Fence, released on hometown label Mammoth Records.
Correction worth making: the song is often misfiled — it comes from Rosemary (1992), and gave its name to the band's Daylight EP later that year; Outside In followed in 1993.
Singer-guitarist Greg Humphreys is the band's principal songwriter; he and bassist Chris Goode first played together in a Winston-Salem high-school band called Trash.
The band took its name from a strange piece of outsider-art fencing Humphreys and guitarist Kent Alphin saw in Dillon, South Carolina, just before their first show.
The lyric runs from darkness to dawn: endless grey nights and ghosts, until 'suddenly there I see the dawn break' — and that one hope is 'the only thing keeping me sane.'
Stereo Review praised the track in 1992 for its 'cascading rush of guitars and bright rainbow of harmonics' behind Humphreys' vocal.
Rosemary was produced by Ron Saint Germain, and critics placed the band straight into the North Carolina jangle lineage of the dB's and Let's Active.
At the time, Dillon Fence were the highest-profile act on Mammoth Records after Juliana Hatfield and the Blake Babies.
The song runs 3 minutes 49 seconds — and tempo trackers clock it at a brisk 140 beats per minute, in A major.
The band split in 1995 but the original lineup has reunited repeatedly since 2001, and 'Daylight' still opens their live sets — it led off their December 2025 show in Greensboro.

title: Hotel California
description: A traveler checks into a glamorous, sinister hotel he can never leave, in the Eagles' defining epic. This official video captures the band live in 1977, closing with the celebrated Felder-and-Walsh guitar duel.

pops.text: Don Felder dreamed up the music in a rented Malibu beach house, layering 12-string guitar over a drum-machine demo.
Henley heard Felder's demo and dubbed its offbeat feel 'Mexican Reggae' — the song's working title.
Felder wrote the music; Don Henley and Glenn Frey shaped the lyrics about the dark side of the California dream.
Henley sings lead from behind the drums while Felder and Glenn Frey both play 12-string acoustics on the studio track.
The album came out in December 1976; the single followed in February 1977 and hit No. 1 on the Hot 100 that May.
This video was filmed live in 1977 at the Capital Centre in Landover, Maryland, on the official Eagles channel.
Joe Walsh, who had just joined the band, trades licks with Felder in the long closing guitar coda.
Henley insisted Felder recreate his year-old demo solo note for note; the pair then spent days perfecting the harmonized parts.
Readers of Guitarist magazine voted that closing solo the best guitar solo of all time in 1998.
The song won the Grammy for Record of the Year in 1978, and the Eagles have performed it live well over a thousand times.

title: You Dropped a Bomb on Me
description: Brothers Charlie, Ronnie and Robert Wilson unleash a synth-funk explosion about a love that hits like ordnance. The camouflage-clad video, complete with animated bomber, is pure early-'80s funk theatre.

pops.text: The Gap Band were Tulsa brothers Charlie, Ronnie and Robert Wilson; GAP stands for Greenwood, Archer and Pine, streets in their hometown.
Charlie Wilson co-wrote the song with producer Lonnie Simmons and Rudy Taylor.
It opens with the whistling sound of a bomb falling — one of funk's most instantly recognizable intros.
The single arrived in August 1982 on Simmons's brand-new Total Experience Records label.
Its parent album, Gap Band IV, topped the Black Albums chart and went platinum, the band's biggest album.
The song climbed to No. 2 on Billboard's Hot Black Singles chart and No. 31 on the Hot 100.
In the video the Wilsons perform in camouflage gear while an animated bomber drops its cartoon payload.
A long-running rumor tied the title to the 1921 Tulsa race massacre; in 2021 Charlie Wilson confirmed that was not the song's inspiration.
Gap Band IV also spun off two R&B No. 1s: 'Early in the Morning' and the much-sampled slow-burner 'Outstanding.'
Charlie Wilson later reinvented himself as a solo star affectionately known to a new generation as 'Uncle Charlie.'

title: We Don't Need Another Hero
description: Tina Turner, in full Aunty Entity chain-mail from Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome, delivers a soaring plea for the children beyond Bartertown. Part film anthem, part power ballad, it became one of her signature hits.

pops.text: Turner didn't just sing the theme — she co-starred in Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome as Aunty Entity, ruthless ruler of Bartertown.
The song was written by Terry Britten and Graham Lyle, the team behind Turner's comeback smash 'What's Love Got to Do with It.'
In the video Turner performs on a lit platform wearing the heavy chain-mail gown of her film character.
Clips from the film are woven through the video, linking the song directly to Max's story.
Released in 1985, the single peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, held off the top by John Parr's 'St. Elmo's Fire.'
It went all the way to No. 1 in Australia, Canada, Spain, Switzerland and West Germany, and No. 3 in the UK.
A children's choir from King's House School in London joins Turner for the song's hopeful finale in the video.
The song earned Turner Grammy and Golden Globe nominations.
Britten and Lyle won the 1985 Ivor Novello Award for Best Song Musically and Lyrically for the track.
The video was nominated for Best Female Video at the MTV Video Music Awards.

title: One Thing Leads to Another
description: A sleek, twitchy new-wave warning about lying politicians, driven by a funky guitar riff and Cy Curnin's clipped vocal. It made London's Fixx far bigger in America than they ever were at home.

pops.text: Singer Cy Curnin has described the song as an indictment of dishonest politicians and the lies that snowball.
The Fixx formed in London in 1979 as the Portraits, with college friends Curnin and drummer Adam Woods at the core.
The track opens the band's second album, Reach the Beach, produced by Rupert Hine and released in May 1983.
Bassist Alfie Agius played on this track but left the band partway through the album sessions.
Released as a US single in August 1983, it became the second of three Top 40 hits from Reach the Beach.
The video became an MTV staple, helping break the British band across the Atlantic.
It peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in November 1983 — still the band's biggest US hit.
The song also hit No. 2 on Billboard's rock chart and went all the way to No. 1 in Canada.
Back home in Britain it barely registered, stalling at No. 86 — the Fixx remained a band bigger abroad than at home.
Reach the Beach reached No. 8 on the US album chart and sold two million copies in America alone.

title: Any Day Now
description: Chuck Jackson pours heartbreak into Burt Bacharach and Bob Hilliard's 'Any Day Now (My Wild Beautiful Bird),' knowing his love will fly away. This official Topic audio presents the original 1962 Wand recording in full orchestral soul splendour.

pops.text: The song was written by Burt Bacharach (music) and Bob Hilliard (lyrics) — before Bacharach's famous partnership with Hal David took off.
Bacharach had orchestrated and recorded the backing track about a year before Jackson sang over it.
That same backing track was first tried out on singer Tommy Hunt's 'Lover,' a version that sat unreleased until 1986.
Jackson had sung with a version of the Del-Vikings before going solo on the Wand label.
Released in 1962 as 'Any Day Now (My Wild Beautiful Bird),' it became Jackson's signature song.
It reached No. 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 and spent six weeks in the Top 40.
On the R&B chart it soared to No. 2, Jackson's biggest hit and his highest-charting pop single.
The song also titled Jackson's 1962 album, Any Day Now.
Elvis Presley cut it in Memphis in 1969, releasing it as the B-side of his hit 'In the Ghetto.'
Ronnie Milsap took it to No. 1 on the country chart in 1982, and Jackson's original later played over the closing credits of the film Inherent Vice.

title: Silly Love Songs
description: Paul McCartney answers critics who called his songs soppy by writing the ultimate love song about love songs — and topping the charts with it. The official video is a joyful tour film from Wings' 1976 world trek.

pops.text: McCartney wrote the song as a rebuttal to critics — and former bandmate John Lennon — who accused him of writing only lightweight love songs.
Paul and Linda McCartney share the songwriting credit, and Linda sings in the stacked counterpoint harmonies.
The arrangement layers voices in counterpoint, a technique McCartney likened to the Beach Boys' 'God Only Knows.'
Under the pop shine sits a disco-funk groove built around one of McCartney's most famous bass lines.
McCartney let the horn section invent their own parts during the Abbey Road sessions.
The single was released on 1 April 1976, backed with Linda's showcase 'Cook of the House.'
This official video was filmed during the 1976 Wings Over the World tour, mixing stage footage with life on the road.
It spent five non-consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Billboard named it the No. 1 pop song of the whole year 1976.
It was McCartney's 27th US No. 1 as a songwriter — a record — yet he has not performed the song live since Wings broke up.

title: Tommy the Cat
description: Les Claypool slaps out a frantic funk-metal tale of an alley cat on the prowl, while Tom Waits growls the title role. The black-and-white video mixes the band, a milk-pouring bartender and rubber-hose cartoon cats.

pops.text: Tom Waits provides the gravelly spoken voice of Tommy the Cat on the studio version; live, Claypool performs both parts himself.
An earlier live version appeared on Primus's 1989 debut album Suck on This, before the band had even met Waits.
The studio version anchors Sailing the Seas of Cheese (1991), Primus's major-label debut on Interscope.
The song is built on Claypool's ferocious slap-bass line, played on his six-string bass.
Songwriting is credited to Claypool, Todd Huth, Larry LaLonde and Tim Alexander.
In the video Claypool plays a bartender pouring milk for the bar's feline customers.
The elderly cat-man in the video was played by Claypool's own grandfather.
Animated sequences show a female cat strutting into an alley full of hopeful tomcats as Tommy tells his tale.
Primus performed the song in the 1991 film Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey, during the Battle of the Bands finale.
Sailing the Seas of Cheese went gold in 1993, and 'Tommy the Cat' remains a rite-of-passage test piece for bass players.
